title: Making a summary you can rely on

sections.skill: Request a source-grounded summary and check it

questions.prompt: Which request is most likely to produce a reliable summary?

choices.text: Asking for "the main points of the news today" with no sources
Asking for a summary of a book you never named
Pasting the article and asking for a summary of it
Asking for a summary of an article from memory without giving the tool its text

questions.correct_answer: Pasting the article and asking for a summary of it
questions.intro: To get a summary you can rely on, SUPPLY THE TEXT and ask the tool to summarize only that text, rather than asking it to summarize something from memory, such as "summarize the novel" or "summarize yesterday's meeting" when it was not given the notes. Say what the summary is for and what it must include ("all deadlines and costs"). Then CHECK it against the source: are the key points there, are they accurate, and is anything added that the source does not say? A good summary saves time only if you can trust it, and trust comes from checking.

sections.skill: Check a summary point by point

questions.prompt: How many key points does the example source have?

choices.text: 1, because it is all about the library and so counts as a single point

questions.intro: Use a quick three-column check. Column 1: each KEY POINT from the source. Column 2: does the summary include it? (yes or no). Column 3: is it ACCURATE? (yes or no). Then scan the summary for anything NOT in column 1 and check whether the source says it. Example source: "Library closes June 1-7. Late fees paused. Return books by May 31." Summary: "Library closed in June; late fees paused." Checks: closure dates partly wrong (not all of June), fee pause correct, return deadline missing.

sections.title: Apply it

sections.skill: Handle summaries of long or important sources

questions.prompt: A 40-page report has 8 sections. How can you make missing parts easy to spot?

choices.text: Ask for a summary section by section
Ask for a single sentence covering all 40 pages so nothing can be left out
Ask for a summary of only the title

questions.correct_answer: Ask for a summary section by section
questions.intro: Long or complex sources need extra care. Ask for the summary in sections that match the source's sections, so missing parts are easy to spot. Ask the tool to quote or point to the source for each key point. For decisions, read the original parts that matter most yourself, such as the cancellation section of a contract or the results section of a study. A summary is a map of the document, and maps leave things out by design.

questions.prompt: What request helps you verify each key point?

choices.text: "For each point, quote the source sentence."
"Be as confident as possible about every point."
